case_info.scenario: A 66-year-old man initially presented to his primary care physician with a persistent cough. A noncontrast chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Subsequent positron emission tomography/CT revealed intrathoracic lymphadenopathy, partially calcified left supraclavicular lymph node, left thyroid nodule, and left level IV neck lymph nodes with calcifications. Mutual analysis of the supraclavicular and left neck lymph node biopsies reported anNCOA4:RETgene fusion, but noBRAF V600Evariant. Left lower lung lobectomy showed tumor cells positive forPAX8,TTF-1, thyroglobulin, andNCOA4:RETgene fusion and negative results for napsin A. Right lower lung lobectomy showed tumor cells positive forTTF-1, napsin A, andNCOA4:RETgene fusion and negative forPAX8and thyroglobulin. Histologically, the supraclavicular lymph node revealed a papillary architecture with nuclear pseudoinclusions and grooves that was identical to the left lung lobectomy (Figure, A). The right lung lobectomy revealed a crowded cribriform glandular arrangement with luminal mucin, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and vesiculated nuclear chromatin (Figure, B).

options.D: Metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma with atypical pulmonary spread

case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

case_info.caption: A, Supraclavicular lymph node biopsy showing a papillary, hyalinized fibrotic nodule with engorged vasculature (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2). case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

B, Right lung lobectomy specimen demonstrating a solid cribriform pattern with eosinophilic cytoplasm (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2).
case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. case_info.caption: A, Supraclavicular lymph node biopsy showing a papillary, hyalinized fibrotic nodule with engorged vasculature (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2). B, Right lung lobectomy specimen demonstrating a solid cribriform pattern with eosinophilic cytoplasm (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2).
case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. case_info.scenario: A 66-year-old man initially presented to his primary care physician with a persistent cough. A noncontrast chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Subsequent positron emission tomography/CT revealed intrathoracic lymphadenopathy, partially calcified left supraclavicular lymph node, left thyroid nodule, and left level IV neck lymph nodes with calcifications. Mutual analysis of the supraclavicular and left neck lymph node biopsies reported anNCOA4:RETgene fusion, but noBRAF V600Evariant. Left lower lung lobectomy showed tumor cells positive forPAX8,TTF-1, thyroglobulin, andNCOA4:RETgene fusion and negative results for napsin A. Right lower lung lobectomy showed tumor cells positive forTTF-1, napsin A, andNCOA4:RETgene fusion and negative forPAX8and thyroglobulin. Histologically, the supraclavicular lymph node revealed a papillary architecture with nuclear pseudoinclusions and grooves that was identical to the left lung lobectomy (Figure, A). The right lung lobectomy revealed a crowded cribriform glandular arrangement with luminal mucin, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and vesiculated nuclear chromatin (Figure, B).

case_info.caption: A, Supraclavicular lymph node biopsy showing a papillary, hyalinized fibrotic nodule with engorged vasculature (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2). B, Right lung lobectomy specimen demonstrating a solid cribriform pattern with eosinophilic cytoplasm (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2).
case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

case_info.caption: A, Supraclavicular lymph node biopsy showing a papillary, hyalinized fibrotic nodule with engorged vasculature (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2). B, Right lung lobectomy specimen demonstrating a solid cribriform pattern with eosinophilic cytoplasm (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2).
case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.
